To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Bayesian reasoning is a skill that can be taught and learned, and that it is improved when people are presented with naturally sampled frequencies rather than single-event probabilities.

(a) the use of naturally sampled frequencies in Bayesian tasks leads to better performance than the use of single-event probabilities, (b) pictorial aids improve performance, (c) individual difference factors also improve performance, (d) the ecological rationality perspective provides a more complete explanation than the heuristic biases view for why naturally sampled frequency and picture aids improve performance, and (e) future research should continue to test and integrate across theoretical perspectives.
Bayesian reasoning improves when the task involves naturally sampled frequencies, pictorial aids, and certain individual differences.

the question of why humans are so poor at Bayesian reasoning, and this paper reviews the current state of the field and offers a path for future research.

Bayesian reasoning is a complex phenomenon that is not well explained by any one theory, and the best approach to studying it is to consider the full range of theoretical perspectives and the empirical evidence for and against each.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the field of Bayesian reasoning is in the midst of such a theoretical integration.
Bayesian reasoning is not just about the numbers but also about the context.
the field of Bayesian reasoning is in the midst of a paradigm shift.
